10098-how-jerusalem-was-won-being-the-re:
W. T. Massey, official correspondent of the London newspapers with the Egyptian Expeditionary Force, published this record of Allenby's campaign in Palestine in London in 1919, with illustrations and maps. It opens with Palestine's influence on the war and its old battlegrounds.

Chapters follow the difficulties of attack, training the army, railways, roads, and the base, preparing for zero day, the Beersheba victory, Gaza's defenses, crushing the Turkish left, and two yeomanry charges. Through Gaza into the open, into the Judean hills, comes the deliverance of the holy city. Readers get a correspondent's full campaign history.
10362-sketches-of-the-east-africa-campai:
Captain Robert V. Dolbey, a Royal Army Medical Corps surgeon, published these sketches in 1918, after service in German East Africa. Dolbey had already written of a regimental surgeon in war and prison, and here he turns to heat, bush, and long marches. His view is that of a doctor near the front, not a general at a map.

Sketches cover Dar-es-Salaam, Pangani River bridges, Handeni water, Morogoro operating tents, and native villages. Wounded Rhodesians, German sisters, and machine-gun porters all appear. Readers get a vivid, humane memoir of a little-known campaign, told with a surgeon's eye.
13573-elizabeth-s-campaign:
Mrs. Humphry Ward's 1918 novel Elizabeth's Campaign, dedicated to the memory of T. S. A. at Passchendaele in October 1917, follows a busy English household in wartime. Sir Henry Chicksands, mounted on his cob, leaves orders for War Agricultural Committee gentlemen, a Red Cross captain, tribunal papers, and a Quaker man's case before riding out.

Gardeners prune roses to flower in February and March, Elizabeth speaks low of a worse submarine return, and talk turns to peace, Lloyd George, and woods ravaged across England. Ward sets a woman's campaign of committee work, gardens, and conscience against the pressure of war news. The novel shows home-front England trying to hold its shape under strain.
21355-middy-and-ensign:
HMS Startler works up the Parang River in the Malay Peninsula in George Manville Fenn's tale. Her screw churns golden foam at the close of a hot day. Aboard her serve midshipman Bob Roberts and ensign Tom Long, whose friendly bickering runs through the book. Tropical illness, insects, and river reptiles plague them both.

The pair cannot tell which local people are friends and which are not. Toll demands on river traffic breed resentment of the British protectorate. Fishing and shooting trips double as lessons in the region's natural history. Their shore fort, built to give the women more room, is nearly taken in their hardest fight.
23829-under-the-rebel-s-reign:
Charles Neufeld published Under the Rebel's Reign in 1900, a story of Egyptian revolt, illustrated by Charles Sheldon. Neufeld, author of A Prisoner of the Khaleefa, sets his tale among soldiers, priests, and prisoners in a land under rebellion.

Chapters move from a quarrel and a fight down the Danube to a surprise and a revelation, then to an encounter on the Nile and a reign of terror in Alexandria. Helmar comes to the rescue, proves his metal, and meets friends again, while Hakesh the priest and prison bars loom ahead. It is a boys' adventure of empire, told with the brisk pace of the period.
30665-gossip-in-the-first-decade-of-vict:
John Ashton put this London book together in 1903, drawing on items from the first ten years of Queen Victoria's reign. He says he lived through that whole reign and gathered his short pieces from many sources, often naming the source for each one. The book also carries pictures made at the time, from cartoons and other drawings of the day.

Its chapters move through the late 1830s and into the 1840s, year by year, with small scenes rather than one long tale. Readers meet the queen's accession and coronation, street life and odd crimes, new railways, the Thames Tunnel flood, and the start of the Houses of Parliament. The mix of court news, crime, sport, and new machines gives a close view of how London felt and talked in those early Victorian years.
31192-from-the-rapidan-to-richmond-and-t:
William Meade Dame, private in the First Company of Richmond Howitzers and later rector of Memorial Protestant Episcopal Church in Baltimore, wrote this 1920 personal narrative of the spring of 1864. Thomas Nelson Page introduces the volume, praising the firsthand witness of a man who had acted in the scenes he depicts.

Four chapters carry Dame from camp life in the winter before the campaign through the Battle of the Wilderness. They continue through the battles of Spottsylvania Court House, and Cold Harbor with the defense of Richmond. Dedicated to his comrades of the Army of Northern Virginia, the sketch gives the Confederate artilleryman's ground-level view of one of the war's hardest campaigns.
31566-lee-s-last-campaign:
Lee's Last Campaign, by Captain J. C. G., was published at Raleigh, North Carolina, by Wm. B. Smith and Company in 1866, entered for copyright in 1865. Its first chapter surveys the condition of the Army of Northern Virginia in its last days. It covers the lines in front of Petersburg, the battles around the city, the final struggle, and the assaults on Forts Mahone and Gregg. Thrilling scenes follow, with the main bodies of both armies standing and looking anxiously on, the Confederate army severed, and the evacuation of Richmond and Petersburg.

The book continues through the greetings of Petersburg ladies to the retreating columns and the retreat itself. Written by a captain close to the events, it is a Confederate officer's account of the war's end in Virginia. Readers of Civil War history will find a compact, firsthand narrative of Lee's final campaign, told from inside the retreating army.
33625-my-first-campaign:
An anonymous volunteer of the Twelfth Rhode Island Volunteers recounts his first campaign in this narrative published at Boston in 1863, copied with little alteration from his private journal. Enlisted on September 16, 1862, and reporting at Camp Stevens in Providence, he served as J. W. Grant, private in Company F. He served under Colonel George H. Browne, from muster in October 1862 until late July 1863.

Written under the hardships of a nine-month campaign, the journal records camp life, marches, and privation as a soldier lived them, rather than as a later history would arrange them. The author published it at his comrades' request, hoping it might serve as a reference for men who could keep no record of their own. It remains a direct, unpolished voice from the Union ranks.
5207-the-guns-of-shiloh-a-story-of-the-g:
Joseph A. Altsheler's Civil War novel follows Dick Mason, a young Northerner who fights with Grant in his first great western campaign. A companion to The Guns of Bull Run, which saw the war from the Southern side. This book opens in flight, moves through mountain lights and telegraph stations, and builds toward the battle of Shiloh itself.

Altsheler mixes invented heroes with historical figures and real battles, including Mill Spring and Fort Donelson along the way. The novel offers young readers a vivid, partisan introduction to the western war, with marching, scouting, and fighting carried at a brisk adventure pace.

govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WGN_WGN: Harold Weisberg wrote to Shari Blair and Paul Brancato on July 4, 1989, asking for tapes. The file name ties the letter to Chicago station WGN. Weisberg spent decades gathering recordings and documents for his assassination research, often by writing to people who had kept them. The short letter is one request in that lifelong collecting effort, sent more than twenty-five years after Dallas.
how-jerusalem-was-won-being-the-record-o:
W T Massey, official correspondent with the Egyptian Expeditionary Force, wrote this record of Allenby's campaign. It was published at London in 1919, with maps and illustrations. Massey follows the army from training and railways to zero day. Beersheba's victory and Gaza's defences open the advance.

Two yeomanry charges and the push into the Judean hills follow. Allenby's official entry into the Holy City crowns the tale. Later chapters make Jerusalem secure and cross the Jordan. Turk positions under the Mount of Olives' guns test the attackers. Massey writes as an eyewitness for the London papers. It is the standard popular record of the campaign.
nasa-tm-19660009046-automatic-flow-chart:
Klaus Hain, of Dynaelectron Corporation in Goddard's Theoretical Division, described a Fortran program that draws flow charts by itself. Good records of complex programs were in growing demand, he notes. Drawing a flow chart by hand took much time, so charts were often skipped. His program does the tiresome drawing work on a plotter device.

The chart shows the logic of a program, with links between its parts. A reader can then follow what the code does without reading every line. Hain aimed to make fair records cheap enough to be routine. In 1965, that idea pointed toward the program documentation tools that later became standard in computing.
nasa-tm-19680008991-snap-8-simulator-loo:
Alfred S. Valerino, James C. Wood, and Joseph F. Reznik, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, document a ground rig in this memorandum. The rig simulates SNAP-8, a nuclear space power system, using real liquid metal loops. Its mechanical design is the subject.

The contents walk through the whole facility. A primary sodium-potassium loop feeds a mercury loop that runs the power cycle. A second sodium-potassium loop rejects the waste heat. Support systems cover vacuum, argon, nitrogen, air cooling, hydraulics, and electrics. Instrumentation gets its own long section. The document is the build record for the simulator.
nasa-tm-19710002792-evaluation-of-failur:
David D. Renz, Ralph J. Zavesky, and Evert B. Hurst of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in November 1970. It studies a failed part on the SERT II spacecraft, the gimbal pin puller. The part failed during vibration testing of the craft.

High-speed films of the tests showed what went wrong. A mix of twisting and axial loads together broke the shear pin, they found. The order of the tests also shaped which failure came first. The redesign slipped a nylon bushing into the joint. That change cut the rubbing load and ended the galling that had scarred the parts.
sketches-of-the-east-africa-campaign: Capt. Robert V. Dolbey of the Royal Army Medical Corps wrote Sketches of the East Africa Campaign, dated 1918 and dedicated to L. A. D. and C. B. The opening pages give one contents entry, Dar-es-Salaam, and a list of pictures. Those pictures name Rhodesians crossing a saved bridge over the Pangani River, shells hitting a German store of shells, a first water supply at Handeni, and an operating theatre at Morogoro. A German dug-out and the old Portuguese watergate at Dar-es-Salaam close the list.
the-guns-of-shiloh-a-story-of-the-great-: Joseph A. Altsheler wrote The Guns of Shiloh, a story of the great western campaign. It belongs to his Civil War Series. Only front matter is present here. It gives a foreword, a list of the series, and a list of principal characters. The foreword calls this book the complement of The Guns of Bull Run. In Bull Run, the war is seen through the eyes of Harry Kenton, on the Southern side. In Shiloh, the struggle is seen through Dick Mason, who fights for the North with Grant.
